tagline: Fields, salt marsh and a Declaration preserved in Exeter.
intro: The American Independence Byway makes a 21-mile loop through Exeter, Kensington, Hampton Falls and Hampton, passing fields, woods and marshes with views of the Atlantic. Visit NH gives the drive about one hour and presents this State Scenic & Cultural Byway as a route through colonial architecture and Revolutionary War heritage.

The loop joins two of New Hampshire’s four original towns with two communities later divided from them. Exeter became a center of revolutionary government after royal governor John Wentworth barred the Provincial Congress from Portsmouth in 1774. The following year, the Congress brought seized provincial records to Exeter, which served as the capital for 14 years. A copy of the Declaration reached Exeter in July 1776 and was read to the town by John Taylor Gilman; that document now anchors the American Independence Museum’s collection.

Begin in Exeter, where the freshwater Exeter River becomes the tidal Squamscott. Kensington lies south of Exeter; Hampton Falls is east of Kensington, followed by Hampton to the northeast. In Hampton Falls, the Taylor and Hampton Falls rivers drain toward Hampton Harbor and the Atlantic. Hampton’s town center meets US 1 and Route 27; Route 27 leads west to Exeter to complete the loop.

moments.title: American Independence Museum
moments.text: A rediscovered Declaration helped turn the Ladd-Gilman House into a museum. The Dunlap broadside surfaced in 1985 while electricians installed a security system. The Society of the Cincinnati explored selling it, but stopped after New Hampshire questioned ownership; the museum opened in 1991. Its collection includes the broadside, two draft copies of the Constitution and a Badge of Military Merit, the original Purple Heart. The campus also includes Folsom Tavern, built in 1775 and moved to its present museum-ground location in 2004. The two buildings occupy a one-acre campus in Exeter, preserving a merchant family’s house alongside the relocated tavern.

moments.title: Kensington
moments.text: Kensington’s Town House occupies a small civic cluster on Amesbury Road, beside two Greek Revival churches. An earlier meetinghouse had become too large for the town’s needs after religious groups stopped using it. It was dismantled, and the present hall was built in 1846 with stones from the old foundation. A 1918 addition brought a stage and proscenium to the main hall. The facade has paired entrances flanking a central window, each doorway topped with a transom. In the 1970s, town meetings moved to a larger American Legion hall, another adjustment as the community’s needs changed.

moments.title: Hampton Falls
moments.text: Nearly 1,000 acres of the Seabrook-Hamptons Estuary’s salt marsh lie within Hampton Falls. The Hampton Falls and Taylor rivers drain the town toward Hampton Harbor and the Atlantic. In a community once occupied with farming and lumbering, falls on the Taylor supplied power for mills. The town is now largely residential, with antique shops along US 1. Its highest ground is Great Hill, 246 feet above sea level, just north of Weares Mill on the Hampton Falls River. The community began as part of Hampton and received its grant as an independent town in 1726.
